questions.prompt: Which benefits does a load balancer provide? Select all that apply.

options.text: Sending requests to less-busy or closer servers (latency)

questions.explanation: A load balancer gives scalability, availability, and better latency. Durability of data is a storage concern, not something a load balancer provides.

questions.prompt: What distinguishes a Layer 7 load balancer from a Layer 4 one?

options.text: Layer 7 is always slower and never used
Layer 7 understands the application protocol and can route on HTTP path, host, headers, or cookies

questions.explanation: Layer 4 routes on IP and port without reading content; Layer 7 reads the application protocol (HTTP), enabling content-based routing and TLS termination, at the cost of more processing.

questions.prompt: Requests vary widely in duration (fast lookups and slow reports). Which algorithm balances them best?
questions.explanation: Least-connections sends each new request to the least-busy server, smoothing uneven load that round-robin would distribute blindly.

questions.prompt: What does a health check let a load balancer do?

options.text: Automatically remove unhealthy servers from rotation and route around failures

questions.explanation: Periodic health checks detect failing servers so the load balancer stops sending them traffic, turning a crash into a non-event for users.

questions.prompt: Why is relying on sticky sessions often a design smell?

options.text: They pin users to one server, so a failure loses their state and load can't rebalance freely

questions.explanation: Stickiness papers over server-side state. Making servers stateless (shared session storage) lets any server serve any user and survive failures.

questions.prompt: A component whose failure takes down the whole system is called a single ______ of failure. (one word)
questions.explanation: A single point of failure (SPOF) is why production runs redundant load balancers — the component that provides availability must not be able to take the system down.
